summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including during Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for partners of any sex. The absence of a ban is not matched by any protection: a March 2024 stakeholder submission by Savie asbl and co-signatories to the country's fifth-cycle Universal Periodic Review records that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights.

Public same-sex affection remains exposed to prosecution. Article 176 of the Penal Code punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by their actions, and local ordinances are applied against LGBTQ people. GayOut's country guide notes there is no explicit national criminalisation while identifying Article 176 and those ordinances as the instruments used against LGBTQ people.

No legal gender recognition exists. Trans people have no route to change their identity documents, and the sources record no gender-identity recognition of any kind.

Relationship recognition is closed. The constitution has banned marriage between partners of the same sex since 2006, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex has no recognition route, and no other partnership status is available.

Violence against LGBTQ people is reported to involve the state's own forces. Queer In The World records violence, harassment and torture involving police, security forces and the army. GayOut reports that armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and that the collapse of state authority in parts of the country leaves legal protections theoretical.

Expression is censored and can carry imprisonment. GayOut rates the country High Risk for LGBTQ+ travellers. Queer In The World advises visitors to keep a low profile and exercise discretion.

Church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral.
tangentialFactors: Human Rights Watch reported on 4 December 2017, on the basis of more than 120 interviews including nine Congolese security-force officers, United Nations officials and 21 M23 fighters, that security forces recruited former M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda between October and December 2016 and deployed them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi. The report records no accountability for the resulting deaths. It is the inventory's only sourced account of how the state's security apparatus treats civilians, and it describes an enforcement environment in which lethal force against civilians goes unpunished.
localsOnly:
For Congolese residents, the absence of a criminal ban on same-sex conduct is not accompanied by any protective machinery. There is no legal gender recognition, so trans people cannot amend identity documents, and no relationship recognition: the constitution has barred marriage between partners of the same sex since 2006.

Enforcement runs through Article 176 of the Penal Code and local ordinances rather than a dedicated anti-homosexuality statute. Residents face violence, harassment and torture involving police, security forces and the army, and in eastern DRC armed militia groups have targeted LGBTQ people with near-total impunity.

Church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral, and LGBT expression is censored with exposure to imprisonment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source prosecution counts or case outcomes under Article 176, so the frequency of enforcement against individuals cannot be stated. No sourced information is available on conditions of detention for LGBTQ detainees, on access to HIV or transition-related healthcare, or on asylum and refoulement practice.

Queer In The World's guidance covers both the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of the Congo; only its DRC-specific statements are carried here, and its country-level risk rating is not broken down by region. GayOut's assessment of militia violence in eastern DRC is not accompanied by incident counts or dates.

Whether a third gender marker or any administrative gender-change procedure exists is unresolved in the inventory; the sources state only that no legal gender change is available.
